clue.text: Touring Britain, once ineffective on either of two frequencies

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the word for ineffective travels round the old name

parts.note: something ineffective is a dud
Alban, like Albion and Albany, is an old name for Britain

explanation.surface: A traveller who once toured Britain and achieved nothing, picked up on two radio wavelengths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touring' says go around. 'Britain, once' is not Albion here but the rarer old form Alban; 'ineffective' wraps around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A radio or phone working on two frequency bands is described with this two-word term.

clue.text: No cheat will overstep it?

indicators.note: the word sits across the boundary between the two clue words, so the letters straddle no and cheat

explanation.surface: An honest darts player will never put a foot over the line.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is tucked across the gap in 'nO CHEat'; the whole clue doubles as the definition, since the oche is the line a darts thrower must not cross.
explanation.definitionFit: In darts the throwing line is called this, and an honest player keeps behind it.

clue.text: Extra virgin

definitions.meaning: extra means spare, left over and not yet called on
virgin as an adjective means fresh, never touched or employed

explanation.surface: Reads like a grade of olive oil on a supermarket label.
explanation.definitionFit: Both spare stock and pristine, untouched material are things nobody has yet put to work.

clue.text: The last word in mattresses on which we'll be completely out

definitions.text: on which we'll be completely out

indicators.note: in places the closing prayer word within the word for mattresses

parts.note: mattresses can stand for beds
amen is the last word said at the end of a prayer

explanation.surface: An advertisement boasting of the ultimate mattress, on which we will sleep soundly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Completely out' suggests sleeping, but it means broke: to be on one's beam-ends is to have no money left.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'on one's beam-ends' means penniless, so the phrase is where we sit when entirely out of funds.

clue.text: Maybe change in layout of linear county

indicators.note: in puts the money word within the rearranged letters
a layout is an arrangement, so the letters of linear are set out afresh

parts.note: change, loose coins, is one kind of cash

explanation.surface: Someone proposes a change to the plan of a long, straight-line shire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' warns that change is only one example of money. 'layout of' rearranges the letters to LANIRE, and 'in' sets the money inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancashire is an English county in the north-west, home to Manchester and Liverpool historically.

clue.text: Widely travelled, carrying protection for flyers

indicators.note: carrying means the two clue words hold the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: A well-travelled person carrying some sort of cover for air passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'widELY TRAvelled'. 'Flyers' looks like air travellers, but it means insects.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the hardened forewings of beetles, which shield the delicate flying wings beneath.

clue.text: Put simply, supremo will block harsh cuts

indicators.note: to block is to sit in the way, so the commander's letters sit within the jumbled word
harsh treatment roughs up the letters of cuts into a new order

parts.note: a supremo is the top commander, the C-in-C or commander-in-chief

explanation.surface: A boss's plain message: the chief will stop savage spending cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'harsh' is an unusual anagram signal, making SUCT; 'will block' sits the commander-in-chief abbreviation in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something brief and to the point is expressed concisely, using few words.

clue.text: Now it's clear … some cricket!

definitions.meaning: perfect eyesight is described as ... vision, so everything is now seen clearly
...20 is the short form of cricket with ... overs a side

explanation.surface: A spectator whose view clears just as some cricket comes into sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both normal sharp eyesight and a quick format of the bat-and-ball game.

clue.text: Through bouncing back filth, answer correspondence …

indicators.note: through means one letter passes within the word turned round
bouncing back means the word for filth is read from right to left

parts.note: filth is slime, sticky dirt

explanation.surface: Wading through a backlash of abuse to reply to one's letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bouncing back' turns SLIME into EMILS, and A goes 'Through' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Electronic messages are the modern form of letters sent and received.

clue.text: … 50% of which heading for evil Fraulein?

indicators.note: fifty per cent means half, here the closing half of the word

parts.note: which points back to the previous answer, the 9-across solution

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Half the messages head to a wicked German young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots link to 9: '50% of' takes the second half of EMAILS, ILS, and 'heading for' adds E from evil.
explanation.definitionFit: A German girl's name, so it fits an example of an unmarried German woman, a Fraulein.

clue.text: Waxy product on counter, it's sustaining champion hairdresser?

indicators.note: sustaining means holding up, so the turned word holds the other letters
counter means running against, so it's is read the other way

parts.note: a whimsical PERM ACE, a champion at perms, as a hairdresser might be called

explanation.surface: A wax product on a shop counter that keeps a top stylist going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on counter' turns IT'S into STI, and 'sustaining' wraps it round PERM ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: This waxy substance from the sperm whale's head was used for candles and ointments.

clue.text: Stop space agency recall of Helen Sharman, for one?

parts.note: NASA is the US space agency

indicators.note: recall means calling back, so the title is read backwards

parts.note: Helen Sharman, the first Briton in space, is a chemist with a doctorate, so a DR

explanation.surface: A space agency calling a halt to the return of Britain's first astronaut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' is the organ sense: a nasard is an organ stop. 'recall of' turns DR into RD.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ register sounding a mutation tone is known as a nasard.

clue.text: Sport finishing early charges not quite a full shilling, conditions irrelevant

indicators.note: charges means rushes into, so the cut sporting word enters the cut phrase
not quite means falling short by the final letter

parts.note: being the full shilling is being all there, mentally sound

indicators.note: finishing early drops the last letter

parts.note: to sport a hat is to wear it

explanation.surface: A sport cut short, charged by someone not quite the full shilling, played whatever the conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims ALL THERE to ALLTHER, 'finishing early' trims WEAR to WEA, and 'charges' sends WEA into it. A shilling was an old British coin; 'not the full shilling' means not all there.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitch or track usable in any weather means the conditions do not matter.

clue.text: One interrupting Head of the UN is an Arabic-French speaker?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
interrupting means breaking into the run of three words

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A delegate interrupting the head of the United Nations in two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: T comes from 'Head of the'; I goes 'interrupting' UNISAN. 'Head of the UN' looks like a single title, but it splits.
explanation.definitionFit: People of Tunisia in North Africa commonly speak both Arabic and French.

clue.text: In bar, everyone passed back 8 nickels

indicators.note: passed back means the whole assembly is sent the other way
in puts the word for everyone within the word for bar

parts.note: a bar of metal is a rod
everyone is all

explanation.surface: In a pub, everyone handed back eight coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 stands for the 8-down answer, TWENTY: twenty nickels make a dollar. R-ALL-OD read backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A nickel is a five-cent coin, so twenty of them are worth a US dollar.

clue.text: Write saying Gold is stocked by a pub West of Exmoor

indicators.note: stocked by means held in the stock of, so the gold goes within the pub group

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house

indicators.note: in an across-written word the west is the leftmost letter

parts.note: OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone writes that gold is kept by a pub on the western edge of Exmoor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West of Exmoor' gives E, so A PH E 'stocked by' OR IS becomes APH-ORIS-E. Exmoor is a moorland national park in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To coin maxims is to compose pithy sayings, which is what the verb means.

clue.text: Element iodine injecting mother of Oscar?

indicators.note: injecting means put into, so the iodine symbol goes within

parts.note: Oscar's mother, or O's mum, playing on O as Oscar in the phonetic alphabet
I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: Someone injects iodine into Oscar's mother, as if in a medical drama.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar is O in the radio alphabet, so his mother is O'S MUM; 'injecting' adds I.
explanation.definitionFit: This dense metal is a chemical element, number 76 in the periodic table.

clue.text: 'Cm' and 'Ra': key when unmasking supplier of narcotics

indicators.note: unmasking strips the outside off, so the phrase loses only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Chemical symbols curium and radium as a key to exposing a drug dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cm' and 'Ra' look like chemistry; just remove the C and Y at the ends of the whole phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The root of this plant yields a narcotic, sedative drug, long used in folk medicine.

clue.text: See 8
In turn, with a net, players seen on it

indicators.note: in places these letters within the pair of short words

parts.note: a turn in a game is a go
a net is a mesh

explanation.surface: Players taking turns with a net, as on a court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' splits the outer pair after its first letter. 'Players' and 'net' suggest tennis, but the players are contestants on television.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiz programme on television features contestants competing for prizes.

clue.text: Supply odd man out

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters of man out are arranged strangely

explanation.surface: Provide the person left over when the group pairs up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd man out' reads as an idiom, but 'odd' scrambles MAN OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A supply of something is a quantity on hand, a stock or sum.

clue.text: As at the outset with development in egg?

definitions.text: As at the outset with development in egg?

indicators.note: the outset of a word is its start, so take its first letter
development means change of form, so in egg is rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering about the first growth stage inside an egg.
explanation.walkthrough: A from 'As at the outset' joins an anagram of IN EGG; the whole clue also describes the process of growing older that begins in the egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Growing older is a development that starts from the egg stage, the beginning of life.

clue.text: Take in Globe ratings going over the top?

indicators.note: in a down clue going over the top places the sailors above the globe word

parts.note: ratings are ordinary sailors, ABs, able seamen
a globe is an orb

explanation.surface: The Golden Globe awards ratings going over the top.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'going over the top' puts ABS above ORB.
explanation.definitionFit: To soak up or digest information or liquid is to take it in.

clue.text: In which suspect is to linger?

definitions.text: In which suspect is to linger?

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious, so the letters are in a dubious order

explanation.surface: A police question about the occasions on which a suspect hangs around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' looks like a noun, the person; it is the anagram signal for IS TO LINGER, and the whole clue describes the lurking.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanging about idly, the acts of a suspect who lingers, are lurkings or dawdlings.

clue.text: Stitch up back and sides

indicators.note: back means the word up is read in reverse

parts.note: R and L are right and left, the two sides

explanation.surface: Sewing up a back seam and the side seams of a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stitch up' looks like a phrase meaning frame, but 'up' gets reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: In knitting this is a stitch made inverted, the counterpart to plain.

clue.text: Nasty flare-up: ref red-carded Scholes?

indicators.note: nasty means ugly, so the letters of flare-up are messed about
a player shown the red card leaves the pitch, so the letters of ref leave the mix

explanation.surface: An ugly flare-up on the pitch: the referee sends off Scholes.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R, E, F from FLAREUP and rearrange the remaining LAUP. Scholes was a Manchester United footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Scholes is the England midfielder, so his first name fits as an example.

clue.text: Name among European set, foremost of socialists

definitions.text: Name among European set, foremost of socialists

indicators.note: among puts the abbreviation for name within the European letter and the jelly word

parts.note: to set like a jelly is to gel

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Pick a name from a European group, the leading socialists.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: Friedrich Engels was a European, among the foremost of socialists.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Engels co-wrote the Communist Manifesto with Marx, a leading figure of socialist thought.

clue.text: Possibly gun concealed by king in Christmas cap

indicators.note: in places the king abbreviation within the festive word
concealed by means hidden inside, so the weapon goes into the festive word

parts.note: Yule is an old name for Christmas
a gun is an example of an arm, a weapon
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A gun hidden by a king inside a Christmas hat, as in a cracker.
explanation.walkthrough: ARM goes into YULE, then K, giving Y-ARM-UL-K-E.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jewish skullcap worn by men is a kippah, also known by this Yiddish name.
